title: Appendix B — The Problem of the Intrinsic (as reflected in the Neo-Aristotelian School)
folder: Burke - The Problem of the Intrinsic
thesis: The intrinsic/extrinsic distinction is not a primitive ontological cut between text and context but a scene-act ratio meta-question: every critical method tacitly determines what counts as 'the work itself' (the intrinsic scene) and what counts as merely 'environing context' (the extrinsic scene), and the choice of where to draw the line is itself a grammatical-rhetorical commitment. Burke uses the Chicago Neo-Aristotelians' polemic against 'Coleridgean' criticism as the occasion to show (a) that the search for purely intrinsic principles drifts historically from Aristotelian ousia through Aquinas's creator-grounded substance through Spinoza's totalizing substance into modern science's purely extrinsic environmentalism — the meaning of 'intrinsic' is unstable across this sequence — and (b) that the right response is not to choose intrinsic-OR-extrinsic but to treat the poem as a constitutive act surviving as an object, requiring both internal-structure analysis and act-scene ratio analysis simultaneously.

outline.heading: Three levels of motive-talk: Rhetoric, Symbolic, Grammar; the intrinsic question as the grammatical entry-point
outline.summary: Burke opens with the doctrine of the 'eternity of art' as a test case. The doctrine can be read rhetorically (defending the antiquarian art-market), symbolically (secular analogue of belief in God's eternity), or grammatically. The grammatical reading reframes 'eternity of art' as the methodological commitment to consider a work 'in itself' — its ascitas, by-itselfness — by analyzing the relation of its parts to one another and to the whole. Burke immediately glosses this in Aristotelian vocabulary: substance is ousia (being); anything considerable hath auto (by-itself) is a substance; treating something in terms of being places it outside the category of time. Even a momentary work can be considered sub specie aeternitatis by attending solely to part-whole relations. This establishes the link: 'intrinsic' = treatable in being-terms = part-whole-only = atemporal/eternal.

outline.heading: Historical drift of 'intrinsic': Aristotle → Aquinas → Spinoza → modern science
outline.summary: Burke traces a four-step historical dialectic in which the meaning of 'intrinsic' progressively inverts into its opposite. (i) Aristotle anchors intrinsicality in the entelechy of the genus: a being's principle is its tribal/familial identity, the aim proper to its kind; the world itself is eternal. (ii) Aquinas retains ousia but, constrained by Genesis, engrafts an extrinsic principle — God as creator — onto Aristotelian substance; intrinsic principles (abilities, habits) are balanced by extrinsic principles (God, the Devil). Burke flags in a footnote that an ancestral God is not wholly extrinsic; the logical completion would lead to pantheism, and Aquinas resists this by classifying God expressly as extrinsic. (iii) Spinoza, applying Aristotle's 'in itself' criterion (id quod per se concipitur) rigorously, concludes that only the totality of being meets the criterion; any finite thing is defined/limited/negated by its surroundings, so genuinely intrinsic motivation can be discussed only at the universal level. Locke makes the parallel etymological point: 'substance' originally means that which supports a thing from outside, not what is in it. Burke's coup: 'the most intrinsic statement we can make about a thing is a statement … about its place as part of the whole world' — meaning 'intrinsic' and 'extrinsic' have nearly traded places. (iv) Spinozistic totalism, once theologically denatured, becomes secular historicism; modern science is par excellence the approach 'from without' — scenic, environmentalist, situational. The category of substance dissolves entirely. Andras Angyal's Foundations for a Science of Personality is the contemporary illustration: a 'science of personality' is a perspective-by-incongruity because the dramatist concept 'personality' is being translated into non-personal terms (organism/environment). The science is therefore necessarily extrinsic in approach.

outline.heading: The Neo-Aristotelian 'Prefatory Note': Crane against the 'Coleridgean' method; the induction/deduction false dichotomy
outline.summary: Burke turns to the three University Review essays (Crane's prefatory note plus Maclean on a Wordsworth sonnet and Olson on Yeats's 'Sailing to Byzantium' — Burke corrects the title from 'Byzantium' implicit in his text to confirm Olson treats Yeats). The Coleridgean method (Crane's target) is characterized as narrowing-down: start with broad philosophical/psychological terms (subjective/objective, extension/intension, structure/texture), progressively descend to particular poems treated as exemplars of broader principles. The result is talk about 'poetry' (touchstones) rather than 'poems.' Maclean and Olson, by contrast, approach lyrics 'as objects' of 'distinctive kind,' inductively, apart from a priori assumptions. Burke counter-argues: critical terminologies are languages; observation is shaped by the analytic vocabulary one brings; pure induction is a 'philosophic subterfuge.' The Aristotelian vocabulary is itself 'dramatist' and 'highly developed,' so the Neo-Aristotelians 'owe too much to the language' to be merely inductive. Without admitting the deductive component, their position is dialectically asymmetric. Their actual practice degenerates into 'prophecy after the event' — rationalization-after-the-fact, a temptation to which Aristotelianism has historically been prone. Genuine induction must 'risk statements as to what to expect, and why,' generalize prospectively, not merely improvise translations of unique poems into unique conceptual paraphrases.

outline.heading: Maclean's Wordsworth sonnet via scene-agent ratio; lyric as state-of-arrest; the action/motion distinction
outline.summary: Burke salutes Maclean's analysis of Wordsworth's 'It is a beauteous evening' as 'spiritual and religious translation of the evening' but argues the analysis would be sharper if explicitly framed as scene-agent ratio. Burke's grammar of the drama already shows that scene-quality contains act-quality (Shakespearean storm-as-setting-for-sinister-act; Hardy's landscape-as-motivation); the same logic applies to scene-agent identification in lyric, where scenic imagery conveys agent-states-of-mind. The sonnet's octave establishes scene-quality (calm, holy, tranquil); the sestet turns to the agent ('Dear Child! dear Girl!'); the agent's quality is so imbued with the divine scene that she possesses the quality unawares — by having it as her ground. Burke then introduces a load-bearing methodological distinction: there are two senses of 'rest.' (a) Rest as cessation of motion (a ball coming to rest) belongs to the physical sciences and motion-vocabulary. (b) Rest as the end of action — end-as-finish or end-as-aim — is Aristotle's primum mobile, the ground of action. The lyric's stasis is rest in sense (b), not sense (a). Treating the human realm in motion-terms yields extrinsic statements only; action-terms are required for intrinsic statements. The lyric is 'a state that sums up an action in the form of an attitude' — attitude being ambiguous between incipient act and substitute-for-act (Keats's Grecian-Urn 'fair Attitude' as summational moment). Burke triangulates the cluster: action, rest (calm/quiet/tranquillity/gentleness), motion, attitude/potential-action. Maclean's gloss on 'free' as 'endowing the evening with the power to act' is rescued: the wholly free is the most tranquil because complete freedom contains action's potentiality without disturbance. Burke runs the same machinery on the 'Tintern Abbey' passage — 'motion of our human blood' (bodily motion) suspended while 'living soul' (mental action) is attained; 'power of harmony' as another synonym for rest-as-potential-action. The Grecian Urn ode is glossed as a similar action/motion split: bodily passion versus mental action, agitation arrested into transcendent counterpart.

outline.heading: Aristotle's two part-whole frameworks; uniqueness vs. genus; Olson on Yeats; Yvor Winters and pseudo-reference
outline.summary: Burke notes that none of the three Neo-Aristotelians mentions Aristotle's two different part-whole frameworks for tragedy (Poetics chapter 6: Plot/Characters/Diction/Thought/Spectacle/Melody as formative parts; Poetics chapter 12: Prologue/Episode/Exode/choral as quantitative parts), and crucially that both frameworks apply to tragedies as a class, not only to individual tragedies. Yet Maclean concludes by stressing the poem's uniqueness, and Olson asserts 'great art is always in the last analysis sui generis.' Burke objects: an 'Aristotelian poetics of the lyric' requires treating lyrics AS A CLASS, which requires terminological prepossessions prior to analysis, even to identify a poem as a lyric in the first place. Placement of any form depends on a vocabulary wider than that form's orbit. The Neo-Aristotelians cannot escape this via the disclaimer that their analyses are merely preparatory — observations confined to the unique are not classificatory. (Footnote: Crane's Coleridge-derived poetry/poem distinction is insufficient; Burke proposes three terms — poetry-as-dialectical-pair-member, poem-as-this-specific-poem, poems-as-class.) Burke then concedes that Olson's actual practice repeatedly profits by violating his stated principle: Olson's generalizations about lyric versus tragedy/epic/comedy ('the kind we have been scrutinizing is static' versus 'dynamic … imitate change') are dramatistic generic claims; his discussion of Yeats is 'thoroughly dramatistic' (action/passion, regeneration, dialectic of transformations across stanzas). Yet Olson presents this vocabulary as forced upon him by inspection of the single poem. Burke endorses Olson's distinction between dramatic 'act' and lyric 'event' and crosses it with his own to produce a footnote-buried theory: the lyric event is more scenic than enactive; scientific events and lyric events are both received as states; hence science:lyric :: impersonal:personal :: materialism:idealism :: scene:agent :: knowledge:knower :: epistemological:psychological. Yvor Winters's 'pseudo-reference' (acts in a chain implying anterior situations whose history is withheld; Eliot's 'Gerontion' example) is reread as 'the very point at which dramatic actions are undergoing transformation into lyric events.' The events are 'moody' — attitude-purveying imagery like storms or sunsets — operating as scenic conveyance of agent-state.

outline.heading: Resolution: the poem as constitutive act surviving as object; intrinsic AND extrinsic via act-scene; Scotist haecceitas and pure-form risk
outline.summary: Burke names the missing third option Crane's dichotomy (exemplar versus object) has suppressed: the poem as act. By looking at the pentad, we may ask 'What about the poem considered as an act?' Crane himself slips toward this when calling the poem 'a product of purposive activity on the part of its author' — Burke agrees 'more intensely than he would want us to.' The crucial move: a poem is a constitutive act; after composition by an agent in a particular temporal scene, it survives as an objective structure examinable in itself, in other temporal scenes, by other agents. The enactment remains as a constitution. This act-into-object framework lets the intrinsic concerns of the Neo-Aristotelians AND the extrinsic concerns of historicist/sociological criticism BOTH have legitimate places: internal structural analysis treats the surviving constitution; act-scene ratio analysis treats the poem's enactment in its original and subsequent scenes. Both are dramatistic. Burke quotes his own Philosophy of Literary Form: words have a nature peculiarly their own AND get a nature from the non-verbal scenes that support their acts; the symbolic-action approach can avoid the excesses of purely environmental schools 'which neglect to trace the structure of the act itself.' Treating the poem solely 'in terms of perfection / finishedness' restricts inquiry; lyrics in particular need cross-poem comparison (one poem qualifies the terms of another) and treatment of individual lyrics 'as stages or stations of a more comprehensive act' — statements about that more comprehensive act being also statements about the intrinsic nature of each. The three levels (Grammar, Rhetoric, Symbolic) are recalled: Symbolic is where modern criticism has 'something vitally new to offer,' and the Neo-Aristotelian compartmentalizing program would obstruct this. The closing footnote pulls in Scotist haecceitas (thisness) — perhaps the Neo-Aristotelians are unconsciously Scotist, extending genus-to-species by a further step from species-to-individual — and warns that the search for pure intrinsicality, completed logically, demands 'pure or separate forms subsisting without admixture of matter,' Aquinas's angels each being both genus and individual at once. Pure-intrinsic criticism risks an angelology of poems.

concepts.label: intrinsic/extrinsic distinction
concepts.gloss: the scope-of-text question — what counts as 'the work itself' versus environing context; Burke argues this is not a primitive ontological cut but a scene-act ratio meta-decision; the very meaning of 'intrinsic' is historically unstable, having nearly inverted between Aristotle and modern science

concepts.label: ascitas / by-itselfness / hath auto / id quod per se concipitur
concepts.gloss: the scholastic-Aristotelian-Spinozistic criterion for treating a being in its own right; Burke uses three vocabularies for the same concept; the criterion drives the historical instability of 'intrinsic' because each thinker who applies it rigorously is forced to a different scope-of-scene (individual / individual-as-creature / totality of being)

concepts.label: ousia / substance / being
concepts.gloss: Aristotelian substance, eternal because treated in being-terms (the relations among parts just are); contrasts with treatment in terms of genesis/history; placing a thing under being-talk is what makes part-whole analysis possible and pulls the analysis outside the category of time

concepts.label: entelechy / that-which-contains-its-own-aim
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's internal principle of motivation as the incentive of a being to attain the perfection proper to its kind; intrinsic-principle anchor in genus rather than in bare individuality; Burke's reading places the entelechy at the level of the tribe/family/class rather than the unique individual

concepts.label: extrinsic principle (God and Devil)
concepts.gloss: Aquinas's engrafted extrinsic ground for substance — derivation from a divine Creator — balanced against the intrinsic principles of abilities and habits; introduces the ambiguity that an ancestral God is not wholly extrinsic, with pantheism as the logical completion Aquinas refuses

concepts.label: Spinoza's totality criterion
concepts.gloss: applying Aristotle's 'in itself' rigorously yields only the universe-as-whole as genuinely intrinsic; any finite being is defined/limited/negated by its surroundings; eventuates in a near-reversal of intrinsic and extrinsic, prepared by Locke's etymological note that 'substance' originally names what supports from outside

concepts.label: secularized historicism
concepts.gloss: Spinozistic equation of nature/God collapses, on theological subtraction, into pure naturalistic history; modern philosophy of science formally abolishes the substance category; the trajectory from Aristotle through Aquinas through Spinoza into modern environmentalist science is the historical dialectic by which 'intrinsic' becomes 'extrinsic'

concepts.label: science as approach from without (scenic/environmentalist/situational)
concepts.gloss: modern science treats human beings in terms of what surrounds and grounds them — animals, vegetables, minerals, electro-physical impulses, climate, food, geography; the gerontologist's 'intrinsic resistance' to aging via chemical dosage is Burke's reductio: the dosage is extrinsic agency, paralleling 'scientific' warming-by-improved-heating rather than by increased cold-resistance

concepts.label: science of personality as perspective-by-incongruity
concepts.gloss: Burke's example: Angyal's Foundations for a Science of Personality builds half its project on organism/environment, terms that 'in their very nature dissolve the concept of personality'; personality is a dramatist concept and a science of it is necessarily extrinsic — at best a 'scientific terminology of the personality' that translates the person into the non-personal

concepts.label: three levels of motive-talk: Grammar / Rhetoric / Symbolic
concepts.gloss: Burke's tripartite division; the intrinsic question is grammatical; rhetorical reading examines doctrines for their persuasive deployment (e.g., antiquarian art-market); symbolic reading examines doctrines as secular analogues of religious patterns (e.g., eternity-of-art as analogue of eternity-of-God); modern criticism's 'vitally new' contribution is on the Symbolic level

concepts.label: 'Coleridgean' method (narrowing-down)
concepts.gloss: Crane's polemical target: critic begins with broad philosophical/psychological frame (subjective/objective, extension/intension, structure/texture), descends through paired contraries to the particular poem treated as exemplar; result is talk of 'poetry' (touchstones) not 'poems'; Burke partially defends as inevitable feature of any analytic vocabulary

concepts.label: Neo-Aristotelian poem-as-object
concepts.gloss: Maclean/Olson approach lyrics 'as objects' of distinctive kind, inductively, without a priori assumptions about poetry-in-general; aim is theoretical grasp of parts of lyrics and principles of unification through inductive accumulation; Burke's critique: pure inductivism is impossible because the Aristotelian vocabulary is already highly developed and shapes observation

concepts.label: induction/deduction false dichotomy
concepts.gloss: Burke's terministic argument: critical terminologies are languages; observation is coached by the terms one brings; the Neo-Aristotelians' inductivism is genuine but supplemented by heavy deductive scaffolding inherited from Aristotle; genuine induction must 'risk statements as to what to expect, and why,' not merely rationalize-after-the-event ('prophecy after the event')

concepts.label: scene-agent ratio (applied to lyric)
concepts.gloss: scene-quality contains agent-quality; in the Wordsworth sonnet the octave's evening-scene (calm/holy/tranquil) imbues the sestet's agent (the Child) so completely that she possesses the divine quality unawares, by ground; the scene-agent ratio is Burke's grammatical principle for lyric just as scene-act ratio is for drama

concepts.label: rest as cessation-of-motion vs. rest as end-of-action
concepts.gloss: load-bearing distinction; cessation-of-motion belongs to physics and to motion-vocabulary; end-of-action (Aristotle's primum mobile, end-as-finish or end-as-aim) belongs to action-vocabulary; treating human affairs in motion-terms yields only extrinsic statements; the lyric's stasis is end-of-action rest

concepts.label: motion vs. action
concepts.gloss: physical sciences treat experience non-dramatically in terms of motion; the social/human requires terms of action or drama; physical sciences are a calculus of events, social sciences a calculus of acts; the social-science error is to appropriate the scenic calculus for charting the act; this is the deep cut underlying Burke's intrinsic/extrinsic methodology

concepts.label: attitude as incipient act or substitute-for-act
concepts.gloss: the lyric's stasis is a state that sums up an action in the form of an attitude; attitude is ambiguous between (a) emotional preparation for an act and (b) substitute that lets intent do service for deed; Keats's Grecian Urn 'fair Attitude' is the summational moment in which action is arrested, made permanent, total; this is the load-bearing extension of the pentad toward the sixth term (Attitude) of the Rhetoric of Motives

concepts.label: lyric as state of arrest / moment of stasis
concepts.gloss: the lyric's defining methodological feature; not analogous to dramatic action but its dialectical counterpart; Burke's example contrast: contemplation of one Station of the Cross is lyric, traversal of the fourteen-Station progression is dramatic; the lyric's special aptitude is erecting a moment into a universe

concepts.label: the universalized poetic 'I'
concepts.gloss: the 'I' that grounds a lyric 'fills the whole universe of discourse'; corollary of action-less, agent-less lyric: where dramatic agents are differentiated by their relation to plot-incidents, lyric character is almost completely universalized; the lyric ground is the only agent, and the agent is the universe

concepts.label: lyric 'event' (vs. dramatic 'act')
concepts.gloss: Olson's distinction Burke endorses and reworks: lyric 'events' are not incidents-connected-by-necessity-or-probability but 'devices for making poetic statements'; in Burke's reframing, events are more scenic than enactive; scientific events and lyric events are both received as states; this yields the proportionality science:lyric :: scene:agent :: knowledge:knower :: epistemological:psychological

concepts.label: Yvor Winters's pseudo-reference
concepts.gloss: Winters's diagnostic for modernist poetry (his 'Gerontion' example): acts denoted in a chain implying anterior situations whose meaning is withheld; Burke reframes pseudo-reference as the 'watershed moment' at which dramatic actions are transforming into lyric events — actions becoming attitude-purveying scenic imagery

concepts.label: poem as act / constitutive act surviving as object
concepts.gloss: Burke's resolution of the intrinsic/extrinsic dilemma: the poem is a constitutive act enacted by a poet in a particular temporal scene, surviving as an objective structure examinable in other scenes by other agents; act-into-object framework lets internal-structure analysis (intrinsic) and act-scene ratio analysis (extrinsic) coexist as complementary, both dramatistic

concepts.label: poem-as-object considered 'in terms of perfection / finishedness'
concepts.gloss: the legitimate intrinsic-pole concern: part-whole relationships of a finished work; Burke endorses this against extrinsicist reductions of the poem to neurosis/physique/diet/climate/cultural-movement/economic-class, but warns that perfection-only inquiry is insufficient because cross-poem comparison and the more-comprehensive-act-of-stages are also required

concepts.label: individual lyrics as stages/stations of a more comprehensive act
concepts.gloss: Burke's move beyond single-work intrinsicality: the terms of one poem are qualified by their use in other poems by the same poet; the corpus-as-whole is a larger act of which individual poems are stations; statements about the comprehensive act are also statements about each poem's intrinsic nature; deflates the sui-generis dogma without abandoning attention to the single work

concepts.label: Scotist haecceitas (thisness)
concepts.gloss: Duns Scotus's principle for the step from species to individual; Burke's closing diagnostic suggestion: the Neo-Aristotelians' insistence on lyric uniqueness 'has somewhat the pattern of Aquinas's doctrine of angels, each of which in his view is both a genus and an individual at the same time'; pure intrinsic criticism risks an angelology of poems — pure forms without admixture of matter

concepts.label: circumference of scene (link to GM-03)
concepts.gloss: the intrinsic/extrinsic question is functionally identical to the choice of circumference developed in GM-03 Scope and Reduction: each candidate intrinsic-boundary (the individual being, the individual-as-creature, the totality, the genus, the species-individual) is a circumference selection; the chapter is the methodological generalization of circumference-choice from scenic to text-scope contexts

concepts.label: substance vocabulary (link to GM-02)
concepts.gloss: the intrinsic/extrinsic essay is the methodological complement of GM-02's substance-vocabulary chapter; intrinsic/extrinsic is itself one of the substance-distinctions developed in Antinomies of Definition (the directional/contextual substance); GM-11 historicizes the distinction across Aristotle/Aquinas/Spinoza/modern science

concepts.label: dramatism as supersession of Neo-Aristotelianism
concepts.gloss: Burke's polemical thesis: 'dramatism' is the trade-name that should replace 'Aristotle' for the Chicago school; the pentad (Act/Scene/Agent/Agency/Purpose) opens the third option (poem as Act) that Crane's exemplar/object dichotomy suppresses; great-name-of-Aristotle has historically stifled fresh inquiry, and the same risk recurs in the Neo-Aristotelian program

concepts.label: 'prophecy after the event' (rationalization-after-the-fact)
concepts.gloss: Burke's diagnostic for what the Neo-Aristotelians' inductivism degenerates into when they abide by their stated principles; not a serious inductivism because real induction must risk prospective generalizations; Aristotelianism has historically been prone to this casuistic temptation

intrinsic_extrinsic_apparatus.description: Burke's operational distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic methods of textual analysis, with the central reframing that this is not a primitive cut but a scene-act ratio meta-decision about scope of scene. Below: definitions, examples, and decision rules extracted from the appendix.

definitions.intrinsic_method: treats the work 'in itself' (ascitas, hath auto, id quod per se concipitur); analyzes division of the work into parts and the relation of parts to one another and to the whole; works in terms of being (ousia) rather than genesis; produces an 'eternal' or 'tenseless' account because part-whole relations just are; book p.465-466
definitions.extrinsic_method: treats the work as situated in a wider environing context (biographical, historical, sociological, ideational, economic, political, climatic, neurotic, dietary, etc.); approach 'from without'; in modern empirical science the extrinsic approach is environmentalist/situational/scenic and dissolves the category of substance; book p.469-470,482
definitions.scope_of_text_reframing: Burke's key move: the intrinsic/extrinsic boundary is itself a methodological choice, not a given; every analysis must implicitly draw a line between 'the work itself' (the intrinsic scene) and 'environing context' (the extrinsic scene); the historical sequence Aristotle → Aquinas → Spinoza → modern science demonstrates that 'intrinsic' has progressively been redrawn to encompass more, until at the limit (Spinoza) only the totality is intrinsic and the original individual-level intrinsic vanishes into the extrinsic; book p.467-469

historical_redrawings_of_intrinsic.intrinsic_scope: the individual being qua member of its genus; the entelechy as principle of perfection proper to the kind
historical_redrawings_of_intrinsic.extrinsic_scope: minimal — the world itself is eternal, no creator-ground
God and the Devil; the ancestral-creator ground; with the ambiguity that an ancestral God is not wholly extrinsic

historical_redrawings_of_intrinsic.intrinsic_scope: only the totality of being meets the 'in itself' criterion
historical_redrawings_of_intrinsic.extrinsic_scope: any finite being's surroundings, which define/limit/negate it

historical_redrawings_of_intrinsic.intrinsic_scope: abolished as a category; science is par excellence the approach 'from without'
the poem-as-act considered as a constitutive enactment surviving as objective structure (internal part-whole relations)
historical_redrawings_of_intrinsic.extrinsic_scope: the poem-as-act considered in its original and subsequent scenes (act-scene ratio)

examples_in_essay.example: Wordsworth, 'It is a beauteous evening' sonnet (Maclean's analysis)
examples_in_essay.intrinsic_treatment_by_Maclean: three-part division of the sonnet and their relation to the whole as 'spiritual and religious translation of the evening'
examples_in_essay.extrinsic_treatment_rejected: earlier critic's anchoring of the sonnet in Wordsworth's biographical reference to his illegitimate daughter (Maclean dismisses)
examples_in_essay.Burke_dramatistic_reframing: octave establishes scene-quality (calm/holy/tranquil); sestet introduces agent (Child); scene-agent ratio identification — agent imbued with divine scenic quality by ground; book p.474-475

examples_in_essay.intrinsic_treatment_by_Olson: object-treatment of the poem as a unique whole of mutually appropriate parts; analysis built around action/passion, regeneration, dialectic of transformations across stanzas
examples_in_essay.Burke_critique: Olson's vocabulary is overtly dramatistic but presented as forced upon him by mere inspection of the single poem; he profits by generalizations about lyric-as-class (lyric static vs. tragedy/epic/comedy dynamic) that violate his stated sui generis principle; book p.479-481

examples_in_essay.Burke_treatment: intrinsic/extrinsic resolution via two-level reading: 'motion of our human blood' (bodily motion) suspended while 'living soul' (mental action) is attained; 'power of harmony' = rest of potential action; the state of arrest is the level of mental action transcending bodily motion; book p.477

the Urn's 'fair Attitude' as the summational moment in which action is arrested; ode constructed about a transcendence wherein bodily passion and mental action split, and a state of agitation is arrested into transcendent counterpart; the urn-as-object is treated dramatistically as urn-as-arrested-act; book p.476-477

the chain of acts implying withheld anterior situations is the 'watershed moment' at which dramatic actions are transforming into lyric events; events become scenic (moody) imagery purveying attitudes; book p.481
diagnostic contrast — concern with the totality of the progression is dramatic; pause-and-contemplation at any one Station, in itself, is lyric; book p.476

examples_in_essay.example: Andras Angyal's Foundations for a Science of Personality
examples_in_essay.Burke_treatment: limit-case of extrinsic method: organism/environment vocabulary dissolves personality into non-personal terms; science of personality is a 'perspective by incongruity'; valuable but necessarily extrinsic; book p.469-470

examples_in_essay.example: gerontologist's 'intrinsic resistance' to aging via chemical dosage
examples_in_essay.Burke_treatment: reductio of confused intrinsic/extrinsic talk; chemical dosage is extrinsic agency, and insofar as it works at all may do so by decreasing rather than increasing intrinsic resistance, parallel to 'scientific' warming-by-heating rather than by increased cold-resistance; book p.469

decision_rules.rule: If the analysis treats only the relation of parts to one another and to the whole, with no reference outside the work, it is operating intrinsically (in being-terms, sub specie aeternitatis); applicable but insufficient for full motive-analysis of the human realm.

If the analysis reduces the work to its conditions of production (biographical, sociological, ideological, economic, neurotic, dietary, climatic), it is operating extrinsically; legitimate but liable to neglect the structure of the act itself.

If the analysis uses motion-vocabulary (cause/effect, stimulus/response, function/environment), it cannot yield statements about the intrinsic; motion-talk produces only extrinsic statements about human affairs.

If the analysis uses action-vocabulary (act/scene/agent/agency/purpose, attitude, motive), it can address the intrinsic — but only by treating the work as a constitutive act whose enactment survives as an object.

An ostensibly inductive analysis that risks no prospective generalizations is 'prophecy after the event,' rationalization-after-the-fact; if it cannot specify what-to-expect-and-why for the class to which the work belongs, it is not classificatory and cannot ground generic claims.

Single-work intrinsicality requires supplementation: the terms of one poem are qualified by their use in other poems by the same poet; individual works are stages/stations of a more comprehensive act, and statements about the comprehensive act are also statements about each work's intrinsic nature.

The dramatistic resolution is poem-as-act surviving as constitution; this admits both internal-structure analysis (intrinsic-pole) and act-scene ratio analysis (extrinsic-pole) without forcing a choice between them.

Pure-intrinsic criticism, if logically completed, demands separated forms without admixture of matter — an angelology of poems (Aquinas's angels each genus-and-individual; Scotist haecceitas as the warning); the dramatistic alternative refuses this completion.

positions.label: Intrinsic/extrinsic is a scene-act ratio meta-question, not a primitive ontological cut
positions.statement: The decision about what counts as the work itself versus its environing context is itself a grammatical-methodological choice about scope of scene; every critical method tacitly draws this line, and the history of 'intrinsic' across Aristotle/Aquinas/Spinoza/modern-science demonstrates the line's instability.

positions.label: The Neo-Aristotelians' inductivism is dialectically asymmetric
positions.statement: Pure induction is a philosophic subterfuge; critical terminologies are languages that coach observation deductively; the highly developed Aristotelian vocabulary the Neo-Aristotelians inherit is itself a strongly deductive instrument, and their refusal to acknowledge this makes their position rhetorically symmetric (against the 'Coleridgean') but methodologically dishonest. Their actual practice is better than their stated principles, profiting by generic dramatistic generalizations they then disavow.

positions.label: The lyric is a state of arrest summing up an action in the form of an attitude
positions.statement: The lyric's defining methodological feature is not the absence of action but its arrest into stasis; lyric rest is end-of-action rest (Aristotle's primum mobile), not cessation-of-motion rest; lyric stasis is the dialectical counterpart of dramatic action, not its analogue; attitude (Keats's 'fair Attitude') is the ambiguous category — incipient act or substitute-for-act — that mediates between action and arrest. This is the load-bearing forward-reference to Attitude as the sixth pentad term in A Rhetoric of Motives.
positions.centrality: load-bearing dramatistic claim, with cross-volume forward reference

positions.label: The poem is a constitutive act surviving as object; intrinsic and extrinsic analyses are complementary dramatistic modes
positions.statement: Crane's dichotomy of poem-as-exemplar versus poem-as-object suppresses the third option of poem-as-act. The pentad pries this open: the poem is a constitutive act enacted by a poet in a particular temporal scene and surviving as an objective structure examinable in other scenes by other agents. Internal-structure analysis treats the surviving constitution (intrinsic); act-scene ratio analysis treats the poem's enactment (extrinsic); both are dramatistic and both are needed.

positions.label: Single-work intrinsicality is insufficient; lyrics must be read as stages of a more comprehensive act
positions.statement: The Neo-Aristotelian commitment to sui generis uniqueness blocks the genus-level generalizations they need to do an Aristotelian poetics of the lyric. Individual lyrics are qualified by their place in the poet's larger corpus; statements about the more-comprehensive-act of the corpus are also statements about each poem's intrinsic nature. This is a partial concession to extrinsic-pole concerns (cross-work comparison) within the dramatistic framework.
positions.centrality: subsidiary resolution; bridges to corpus-level analysis

positions.label: Pure-intrinsic criticism risks an angelology of poems
positions.statement: Logically completed, the demand for fully intrinsic criticism requires pure forms subsisting without admixture of matter — Aquinas's angels each both genus and individual at once. The Neo-Aristotelians' insistence on lyric uniqueness combined with their search for the lyric as a kind tracks this Scotist haecceitas/angelology pattern, perhaps as a return to scholasticism by way of modern empirical science. The dramatistic alternative refuses this completion by reinserting the matter — the scene of enactment.

tensions.label: Inductive purity versus inherited deductive vocabulary
tensions.description: The Neo-Aristotelians stake their dialectical position on a contrast between their inductivism and the Coleridgean narrowing-down, yet they inherit the most heavily developed dramatistic vocabulary in the philosophical tradition (Aristotle's Poetics); their actual practice deploys generic claims that violate their stated sui generis principle. Burke's diagnostic — Olson's better passages 'profit by going beyond his principle of uniqueness' — exposes this tension as productive rather than fatal, but unacknowledged.
tensions.burke_resolution: admit the deductive component, treat critical terminologies as languages, treat induction as risking-prospective-generalizations rather than rationalizing-after-the-event

tensions.label: Intrinsic-as-individual versus intrinsic-as-totality
tensions.description: The historical sequence shows the same 'in itself' criterion driving incompatible scopes: Aristotle locates intrinsicality at the individual-as-member-of-genus; Spinoza locates it at the totality of being; Aquinas tries to balance them; modern science abolishes the category. The same criterion thus produces near-opposite extensions. This is the deepest tension in the chapter and the one Burke uses to argue that intrinsic/extrinsic is methodologically chosen, not given.
tensions.burke_resolution: the choice of intrinsic scope is itself a scene-act ratio meta-decision (link to circumference in GM-03); the dramatistic alternative is to treat the poem as constitutive act, which sets both scopes simultaneously

tensions.label: Action versus motion in lyric stasis
tensions.description: The lyric's defining feature is arrest, but 'rest' is ambiguous between cessation-of-motion (physical science) and end-of-action (Aristotelian primum mobile). The Neo-Aristotelians' insistence on lyric-as-static risks collapse into the motion-vocabulary side, which would make the lyric a non-dramatic phenomenon and align it with science. Burke instead aligns lyric stasis with end-of-action rest, preserving its dramatistic character.
tensions.burke_resolution: two senses of rest must be distinguished; lyric is end-of-action rest, mediated by attitude as incipient-act or substitute-for-act; lyric events are scenic but received as states, hence the science:lyric proportionality

tensions.label: Sui generis uniqueness versus generic classification
tensions.description: An Aristotelian poetics of the lyric requires treating lyrics as a class; Maclean and Olson conclude with strong sui generis claims; this would block classificatory analysis. The tension is acute because both Aristotle's Poetics chapters 6 and 12 treat part-whole relationships as applying to tragedies as a class. Burke argues the Neo-Aristotelians' practice is better than their stated principle.
tensions.burke_resolution: individual works are stages/stations of a more comprehensive act; statements about the comprehensive act are also statements about each work's intrinsic nature; uniqueness and generic placement coexist

tensions.label: Dramatism in form versus disavowal in name
tensions.description: Olson's analysis of Yeats deploys an explicitly dramatist vocabulary (action/passion, regeneration, dialectic) yet warns against treating lyric imagery as analogue of dramatic plot. He is dramatist in practice and anti-dramatist in nominal commitment. The tension is the rhetorical signature of the Chicago school's relation to Burke's own apparatus.
tensions.burke_resolution: rebrand the practice — 'these men ply their trade under the trade-name of dramatism rather than Aristotle'; embrace the pentad including the suppressed third option of poem-as-act

dissertation_deployment.dramatistic_resolution_for_games: The game-as-act framework — analogous to Burke's poem-as-constitutive-act-surviving-as-object — lets the dissertation hold the intrinsic-pole (the artifact's internal structural logic, its rules and systems) and the extrinsic-pole (the game's enactment by players in particular scenes, its scene-act and scene-agent ratios across communities) simultaneously, without forcing a choice between formalist game studies and contextualist game studies. Each playthrough is the game's re-enactment by new agents in new temporal scenes; the artifact survives as constitution; intrinsic analysis treats the surviving constitution, extrinsic analysis treats the re-enactment.
dissertation_deployment.rest_two_senses_for_games: The two-senses-of-rest distinction is directly portable: cessation-of-motion analysis (the player put down the controller; the avatar stopped moving) is motion-vocabulary and yields only extrinsic statements; end-of-action analysis (the quest is completed; the build is optimized; the run is finished) is action-vocabulary and yields intrinsic statements about the game's motivational structure. The distinction sharpens the methodology of game-studies analyses that conflate these — e.g., engagement-metric studies that treat input-frequency (motion) as if it were act-of-playing (action).
dissertation_deployment.attitude_as_sixth_term_for_games: The attitude-as-incipient-act-or-substitute-for-act category from p.476 is the methodological pivot toward Burke's 1950 sixth-term apparatus and is directly portable to game-user comportment: many game-affordances elicit attitude without enacting (the held-but-not-pressed button; the camera-pan to a quest objective the player chooses not to pursue; the menu-open contemplation). Attitude-as-incipient-act maps onto Calleja's affective involvement dimension; attitude-as-substitute maps onto the spectator-mode/let's-play viewer.
dissertation_deployment.comprehensive_act_for_game_corpora: The comprehensive-act-of-stages framework licenses treating a developer's oeuvre (FromSoftware's Souls series; Nintendo's Mario lineage; an indie auteur's catalog) as a more-comprehensive-act of which individual titles are stations; statements about the comprehensive act are also statements about each title's intrinsic nature. This is the dramatistic warrant for franchise-level critical analysis.
